articles.title: Who speaks for the voiceless in Tanzania?
articles.author: Zita Zage
paras: ‘All we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.’
Originally published on Global Voices
Jhiko Manyika performing at Zanzibar Reggae Festival. Image by Zanzibar Reggae Festival, used with permission.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.
When courts stop protecting people, people stop talking. They stay quiet because speaking up could cost them their lives or their families. So who speaks for the voiceless?

In Tanzania, one answer comes with a guitar. Reggae artist Jhikoman, born Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika, has released a song called “Justice,” written for everyone who lost a loved one, and the right to mourn them out loud, after the October 2025 general elections that declared Samia Suluhu Hassan president.
His favorite lyric sums up the song:
“We don’t need no war, all we want is peace; there will be no peace without equal rights and justice.”
Tanzania’s image shattered

For nearly six decades, Tanzania cultivated an image of calm, consensus, and order. The scale of the 2025 election violence shocked many people because it broke that image. The BBC reported that security forces and unrest killed more than 500 people. International observers criticized the vote for its lack of transparency, and the African Union and the Southern African Development Community (SADC) said the election fell short of democratic standards.
Jhikoman, who watched these events unfold, says the losses moved him to write. He told Global Voices:

“I was deeply moved by reports and accounts of people losing their lives, families losing their loved ones, and citizens being silenced by the authorities when they simply wanted to speak out, seek answers, and mourn those they had lost. That pain became my motivation to write ‘Justice.’”
This song is more than a song; it is a cry for humanity, a call for accountability, and a reminder that the pain of those who have lost loved ones should never be silenced.
A reggae musician from Bagamoyo

Every stage name has a story, and Jhikoman’s is no different: JHIKO (from his first name, Jhikolabwino) plus MAN (from his surname, Manyika). Jhikoman has performed since 1994, blending acoustic reggae with African music and singing in English, Swahili, and his mother tongue, Kinyasa.

His musical life started at home. His older brother played guitar, and young Jhikoman watched, listened and dreamed. In secondary school, he fell for reggae, drawn by its messages of peace, love, unity, equality, and justice. He idolized Bob Marley and Alpha Blondy, and he covered their songs. Then his brother gave him the advice that changed everything: If you want to be a musician, write your own songs.
Jhikolabwino Siza Manyika performing at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. Photo by Micky Grapher, used with permission.

He took the advice to heart. In 1994, he stepped into a recording studio for the first time. In 2000, he released the album “Afro-Caribbean Beat,” and its title track became a local hit. The opportunities followed quickly. In 2001, he performed at the Zanzibar International Film Festival. In 2003, he wrote a song for Participatory Ecological Land Use Management (PELUM) Tanzania, an organization that supports small-scale farmers, and the commission took him to South Africa to perform at the World Forum for Sustainable Development. Since then, his music has carried him across East and Southern Africa and to stages in Europe.
Today he lives in Bagamoyo, where he volunteers as a music instructor at the Bagamoyo Institute of Arts and Culture and mentors young artists. He says:
“For me, music is more than entertainment. It is a powerful tool for communication, education, unity, and social change.”
The violence after the 2025 general election touched Jhikoman’s own circle. He says police shot and killed the wife of a close friend while she drove home, in front of her two children. He noted:

“No innocent person should lose their life simply because of violence surrounding an election. The victims and their families deserve justice, dignity, and the freedom to mourn without fear or intimidation.”

According to Jhikoman, the people who spoke out and wanted democratic reform often got silenced. They called for changes to election laws and procedures that would guarantee free, fair, transparent, and credible elections. They also demanded equal opportunities for all political parties, independent electoral oversight, and the freedom to choose their leaders without intimidation.
Why it’s so hard to get justice

Article 18 of Tanzania’s 1977 Constitution guarantees freedom of expression. Jhikoman says that some victims and their families have tried to enforce that right in court. However, getting justice has proved “extremely difficult.”

He points to several cases. After the alleged abduction of opposition activist Mpaluka Nyagali, known as Mdude, in May 2025, his wife filed a habeas corpus petition at the High Court in Mbeya. The court dismissed it on July 9, 2025, and his whereabouts remained unknown. A lawyer for former ambassador Humphrey Polepole filed a similar application after he disappeared in October 2025, and the court dismissed that as well.

Two advocates, Tito Magoti and Bob Wangwe, filed a case at the East African Court of Justice challenging the conduct of the election, and it remains pending. Authorities also arrested Tundu Lissu, chairman of the opposition party CHADEMA, and charged him with treason after he demanded electoral reforms. On November 6, 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason, convicted him of incitement, and sentenced him to four years in prison. He remains imprisoned.

“The law guarantees freedom of expression, but people who criticize the government face arrest, intimidation, and, in some cases, alleged abduction. The central problem is not simply the absence of laws; it is the difficulty of holding those responsible for violations accountable.”
A song that carries a message abroad

Listeners have responded well to Jhikoman’s message. He says that many Tanzanians feel the song finally carries their message to the international community. They believe the judiciary and parliament have lost their independence, which leaves them with little confidence that local institutions will deliver justice. Many now place their hope in international attention, because Tanzania has signed numerous international human rights agreements.
Some listeners also worry about his safety. They urge him to take care, since abductions and enforced disappearances remain serious concerns in parts of East Africa.

“I take those warnings seriously,” he says. “But I also believe that music can be a powerful tool for speaking out, raising awareness, and standing up for peace, justice, and the dignity of human life. … True peace means treating one another equally, standing up against injustice, respecting human rights, and giving everyone the freedom to express themselves without fear.”

Jhikoman’s story shows how justice shapes daily life long before anyone reaches a courtroom. When people trust that the justice system will treat them fairly and quickly, they speak out, report wrongdoings, and rebuild after loss. When they lose that trust, silence spreads. One reggae song cannot repair broken institutions, but it can name the problem, keep the memory of the dead in public view, and ask listeners to hold their leaders accountable.

articles.title: Russia wants to build a new security framework to end the war. This is why it won’t work
articles.author: Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva, Lecturer - National Security College, Australian National University
paras: When negotiators from Russia, the United States and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi recently for peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, the Russians pushed a long-held demand for a new security architecture for Europe. Washington has appeared open to this, with US President Donald Trump touting a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”.
While little was revealed about what such a framework would look like specifically, a recent speech by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov provides some clues.
At a security conference in Minsk, Belarus, earlier this month, Lavrov proposed a new security architecture for the entire Eurasian continent.

Reiterating the claim Russia has long made to justify its war in Ukraine, Lavrov said NATO had repeatedly pledged not to expand eastward to contain Russia, but did so anyway. And, he said, the West is now pursuing a new “NATO-style military-political bloc in Asia”.
In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War.

A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added:
If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready.
A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical.

The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance.

And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either.

That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests.
In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia.
This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities.

Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides.
Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders.
Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision.

Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order.
As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities.

Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence.
What the rest of Asia wants

Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others.

Each of these groupings has its own distinct strategic interests and priorities. So, it remains unclear how a new Russia-led security framework would interact with these groups, or potentially compete with them.

Indeed, there seems to be a growing preference, especially in Asia, for smaller alliances between countries with similar ideological world views, such as the new security pact between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey.

At the same time, other nations, particularly those in Southeast Asia, have held fast to their non-aligned status, preferring to seek partnerships with an array of countries that suit a variety of interests.
We may be witnessing the gradual erosion of the post-second world war international order. Now, the big question is what comes next.
While Russia’s aims seem reminiscent of Soviet influence during the Cold War, this is a new world, and there are too many hurdles for its vision of a new security framework to become a reality.

New international orders do not emerge overnight. Rather, they evolve through the cumulative decisions of states pursuing their own interests, forming new alignments, alliances and partnerships along the way.
Dilnoza Ubaydullaeva receives funding from the Japan Foundation Program.

articles.title: Support Global Voices’ January Spotlight: Independent journalism
articles.author: Global Voices Announcements
paras: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Image made via Canva Pro. All images fair use.

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile.

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

articles.title: Elon Musk has approval to launch 1 million satellites. An astronomer explains how this would impact the sky
articles.author: Michael J. I. Brown, Associate Professor in Astronomy, Monash University
paras: This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “Starmind” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation.
If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places.
SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth.
But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit?
We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature.

The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000.
But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites.

To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day.

This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences.

When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors.
Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers.
Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky.
If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon.
Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change.

Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are.
The orbital clutter comes with real risks.

Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable.

Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail.
Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger.

The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts.

However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”.

There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.

This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “Dyson sphere” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy.

One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process.
Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do.
Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat.
And apart from the physics there’s the finance.
Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues. And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth.
If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth.

articles.title: Can the International Criminal Court survive Trump’s attacks – and hold world leaders to account?
articles.author: Grace Jennings-Edquist, Executive Producer, Podcasts, The Conversation
paras: More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague.
Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs.
The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution.

“Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast.

The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries.
McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals.

In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says.
The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court.

“The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it.

Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC.

While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says:
There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states.
Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall.
Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date.

McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order.
“I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says.
McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order:

It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers.
Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC.
I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court.

articles.title: Is Russia about to launch a nuclear weapon into Earth’s orbit? A space law expert explains the threat
articles.author: Art Cotterell, Postdoctoral Fellow, Faculty of Law & Justice, UNSW
paras: As early as December. That’s how soon Russia could put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to German media reports.
If the news sounds familiar from headlines past, that’s because it is. In 2024, the United States made a similar allegation, albeit without giving any potential launch window.
These latest reports claim that the satellite, Sputnik-S, was assembled several years ago and is in storage near Moscow.

Intelligence agencies in NATO countries have reportedly shared information about the satellite. This week, the alliance’s secretary general asserted that protecting NATO territory includes keeping it safe from threats to space systems.

Russia’s embassy in Berlin said it “categorically reject[s] all these groundless allegations”. Echoing Moscow’s 2024 denial, it called the reports “propaganda”, adding that Russia “strictly adheres to the fundamental 1967 Outer Space Treaty”.
What is this treaty and what does it say about nuclear weapons? And how could the international community respond or even verify what is on board a satellite?
The prospect of nuclear weapons off-Earth helped drive negotiations for the treaty invoked by Russia.

During the Cold War, the US and the Soviet Union found common ground on keeping these weapons out of orbit. It was a lesson on cooperation, despite competition and conflict, worth recalling in what is framed as today’s “space race”.
A cornerstone of international space law that prevails to this day, the Outer Space Treaty is also an arms control treaty. Under Article IV, countries undertake not to:

place in orbit around the Earth any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, install such weapons on celestial bodies, or station such weapons in outer space in any other manner.

Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit would itself breach the prohibition, even if it was never detonated. If a detonation did occur, it would breach the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty of 1963, which prohibits nuclear explosions in outer space and in the atmosphere.
No country is known to have ever placed a nuclear weapon in orbit. But there are examples from history of states detonating nuclear weapons off-Earth.

One summer’s night in 1962, people in Hawai'i gazed upward and saw what was, in effect, a nuclear “aurora”. One eyewitness, then a teenager, who was watching with her sibling from a spot overlooking Pearl Harbor, recalled the “exploding sky” and how it later turned “a deep blood red that lingered”.
The US had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometres above the Pacific Ocean in a classified test code-named Starfish Prime.
The US and the Soviet Union were testing nuclear weapons in space almost in lockstep, each demonstrating its advancing technological capabilities.
Starfish Prime was more than a visual spectacle. Of the 24 satellites in orbit at the time or launched in the following weeks, at least a third suffered damage.
What happens in space is a threat on Earth
Today, the European Space Agency estimates there are about 15,800 functioning satellites in Earth’s orbit.

These satellites support the critical infrastructure we rely on every day, from navigation for transport to timing for banking and telecommunications. Whether we realise it or not, we are all “space citizens”.

Some satellites also support nuclear command, control and communications functions. Others give early warning of missile attacks. Researchers at the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute examine this “space–nuclear nexus”.

During a conflict, leaders might interpret an attack on an early-warning satellite as “a precursor to a nuclear-first strike”. How they respond to that ambiguity could have escalatory risks and significance.
Mitigating the threat through verification
So, what can the global community do to mitigate possible and actual threats of nuclear weapons in space?

As a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, Russia could veto a resolution responding to the current allegation. Indeed, in 2024, it vetoed a US–Japan draft resolution reaffirming the Article IV prohibition.
The Outer Space Treaty sets out no specific procedure for verifying whether a satellite carries a nuclear weapon, nor does any other international instrument.

Three think tanks working on global and space security have led expert dialogues on how to do so. In their latest joint report, they conclude that verification is “feasible”, albeit challenging, and should be pursued even if “progress may be incremental”.

The report canvasses multiple options. These include nations working together to test ways of detecting a nuclear weapon in orbit, agreeing on how to handle disputed evidence, and inviting pre-launch inspections.
In my research, I have been exploring how nuclear safeguards could advance non-proliferation by verifying nuclear material on board a space object before launch.

As global nuclear arsenals continue to expand and modernise, we must not lose hope of a world one day free of nuclear weapons, an aspiration reflected in the disarmament pillar of the Non-Proliferation Treaty of 1968.
The onus must also rest heavily on states actually capable of launching nuclear-armed satellites, whether or not they face allegations.
The US, China and Russia could discuss verification options in the trilateral dialogue they recently agreed to hold on nuclear risk.

In a strained geopolitical context, a nation’s verbal reassurances alone are unlikely to give the global community the confidence it needs. Nations agreed nearly 60 years ago to keep nuclear weapons out of space.
Verifying whether they keep that commitment will take cooperation, too.
Art Cotterell's postdoctoral fellowship is co-funded by the UNSW Nuclear Innovation Centre and UNSW Law & Justice. He is affiliated with the Australasian Centre for Space Governance.

articles.title: Using AI to hunt for Black Friday bargains? That ‘great deal’ might not exist
articles.author: Jeannie Marie Paterson, Professor of Law (consumer protections and credit law), The University of Melbourne
paras: To get the most out of Black Friday sales, a bit of research is always useful. Ideally, this involves working out what you might want to buy – and checking prices – before sales begin.
Once the sales are under way, comparing prices, delivery costs and delivery times at different stores can feel onerous and time-consuming, especially if you’re worried you might miss out on a deal.
To streamline their search for a bargain, some shoppers are turning to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to do the research for them.
Can AI really help you snag a deal? The answer is yes, maybe. But there are reasons to proceed carefully.
Sending bots on a bargain hunt
AI is being used to take the legwork out of all sorts of tasks. It makes sense consumers across the world are increasingly putting it to work as a shopping companion.

Say you’re looking for a new coffee machine or laptop this Black Friday. Rather than trawl through dozens of different sites yourself, you might ask a tool such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini to search the web for you and prepare a spreadsheet with a list of options.
A recent survey by the Australian Retail Council and market research firm Roy Morgan found this Black Friday, one in four respondents were planning to use an AI chatbot for research.
Among this group, 72% said it would be their first time doing so. If you fall into this category, there are a few things to be aware of as you check any recommendations.
Bogus bargains, ‘ghost stores’ and ads
Hallucination is a well-known feature of generative AI tools. In the context of shopping with AI, this means some products, prices and stores may be entirely made up or misinterpreted.
A related concern is whether AI tools can reliably distinguish between genuine online stores and the fake or “ghost stores” that spring up online during sales periods.
Then, of course, there’s advertising.
Many AI tools, including the free and low-cost versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Google Search’s AI Overview and AI Mode, have already started rolling out advertising.
Both OpenAI and Google say advertisements shown to users are clearly labelled. But depending on your settings, the ads you see may be informed by your previous conversations with these tools.
Other generative AI tools don’t have ads. Anthropic, for example, has pledged to keep Claude ad-free. And Google’s Gemini app remains free of advertising, at least for now.
The other side of the checkout
Even if you decide not to use AI this Black Friday, it could still shape the deals you see. Some retailers are reportedly already using AI to guide their discounting strategies.
This includes using sophisticated models and past sales data to work out the smallest discount they need to offer to sell a product.
Another potential headwind for shoppers is the use of AI by retailers to personalise prices to the amount a consumer is likely to be prepared to pay, sometimes called “surveillance pricing”.
Currently, this is not explicitly against the law unless the surveillance pricing involves discrimination based on protected characteristics such as race, sex or disability.

By Black Friday next year, new tools which go beyond simple research may be more commonplace: AI shopping agents. These tools can find stores selling what you’re looking for, compare prices and then complete the purchase on your behalf.
For example, Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in Australia last week, integrates with existing social media accounts and can complete tasks on your behalf.

Other tech companies are also venturing into the space. OpenAI recently launched its Dots agent, and Google’s offerings include Agentic Checkout and Gemini Tasks. Amazon offers its own shopping agent but blocks other third-party agents from accessing its site.
Developers such as Meta say they are building in protections to prevent consumer AI agents “going rogue” and overstepping their authority or spending instructions.

But even with safeguards in place, other risks could be amplified. AI agents rely on “context” to execute the purchases their consumers are likely to prefer. Essentially, this means information about your previous interactions is used to predict what you might want in the future.

More broadly, there is the risk AI tools may not be working in shoppers’ best interests. An OECD paper this month warned commercial partnerships could shape which products and prices AI tools recommend, in ways that may not be understood by shoppers.
The federal government has flagged new laws may be needed to respond to the rise of AI shopping agents, including to guard against manipulation or exploitative personalised pricing.
Some old-fashioned common sense
So, what’s the advice? By all means, use AI to find a Black Friday bargain, if you choose. But be sceptical. Treat its recommendations as just one piece of information.
It is worth checking the policies of your preferred AI tool to see if you can turn off its memory of earlier chats.
You may also be able to limit advertising and prevent your prompts from being used for training.
Ultimately, getting the best deal still means weighing up your options, sticking to a budget and thinking about whether you really need what’s on sale.
Jeannie Marie Paterson receives funding from the Austrlian Research Council and the Medical Research Future Fund.

articles.title: Jailed for being poor, forgotten by slow courts in Nigeria, saved by strangers online
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home
Originally published on Global Voices
Court of Appeal building in Lagos, Nigeria. Image by King ChristLike via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post by Fatima Zahra Yahaya is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In February 2025, a letter from a jailed man named Thomas Jonathan Biodun reached the public after some Nigerian Twitter influencers visited his prison to play a friendly football match with the inmates. Biodun was in jail over a debt of NGN 1,137,000 (USD 758). In the letter, he said he had asked for help online before, but someone had called him a scammer.

One of the influencers shared the letter on social media. Another influencer, Sir Dickson, who goes by the handle Wizarab10 on X, pushed it further, garnering over 2.5 million views in one post. In his post, Sir Dickson said, “Nobody should be in prison over a debt. It is not a criminal offense. I have spoken to @egi_nupe [another X influencer and lawyer], and we will be taking it up. Imagine rotting in prison because you’re poor.” A public donation campaign followed, and within weeks, it had raised enough money to clear the debt.
Punch Newspapers reported that Biodun walked out of Apapa Kirikiri Correctional Center and thanked everyone who helped.
Biodun’s story has a happy ending. But it raises a hard question: Should a person’s freedom depend on the benevolence of internet strangers and how many people share a post?
The problem behind this story

In February 2026, the Nigerian Correctional Service said that most people in its custody were still waiting for trial. Many of them have not been found guilty of any crime but remain in pre-trial detention. While some of them cannot pay bail, others cannot pay court fines. In Nigeria, the crime of being poor can land you in a jail cell.

Waiting is not a small thing. While a case drags on, a person may lose their job, business, or place to live. A family can lose its breadwinner, which can derail a whole family — or even a whole community’s livelihoods.
When the internet steps in
Jonathan Biodun is not the only person who turned to the internet to seek support for injustice.

Quadri Alabi, 17, went viral in 2023 when he stood in front of former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s campaign convoy. He spent months in Kirikiri Prison over a robbery charge that his lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, called baseless. Effiong also said the police recorded him under the wrong age, meaning he was charged and sentenced as an adult. On April 17, 2025, he was freed. The same day, Effiong asked the public on X to help his family move to a safer home, because they were still getting threats. The International Center for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that more than NGN 3 million (over USD 21,965) was raised within two hours.

Emeka Nzeruike was arrested in 2015, when he was only 12 years old, over an alleged theft. He spent 10 years in prison waiting for trial. In July 2025, a lawyer named Alexander Nzeadi, who posts on X as @_youfoundalex, took up his case, and Emeka walked out of court.

The lawyer wrote that Emeka had been alone, afraid, and forgotten, with no trial and no lawyer. He then asked Nigerians to help Emeka heal, learn a skill, and start his life again now that he was finally free. The post was seen millions of times.
The other side of the story

Look closely at these cases. Biodun, Alabi, and Nzeruike were helped because their stories reached the right people. A letter found the right hands. A lawyer or a kind stranger posted at the right time.
Biodun said he was first called a scammer. That shows how difficult it can be to be believed online.
But what about the person nobody posts about? Not every inmate has a famous friend, a lawyer, or a loud voice to advocate on their behalf. For them, it can feel like no one is watching.
This is the worry. If help comes only to the stories that go viral, then luck decides who goes home. A sad story with a clear photo may win hearts, while a quiet case may be missed.
Raising money to pay for inmates’ legal fees or fines is not new, and it is not only done online.

In 2023, The Conclave reported that public-spirited people and a group called Prisoners Rehabilitation and Welfare Action (PRAWA), a non-governmental organization (NGO), paid fines to free 37 inmates from Kuje and Suleja prisons. The Interior Minister at the time had urged Nigerians to pay the fines of some prisoners to ease crowding in prisons.
Kindness is good. But justice should not depend on luck or others’ generosity.

I do not believe we should stop being kind. I believe we should fix the courts, so that kindness is not the only hope a poor person has. If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home.
Social media is already doing one useful thing. It shows us real faces and real stories where the system is failing. Smart leaders, lawyers, and judges can listen, and they can fix it.
Until then, every shared post is a sign that Nigerians care. It is also a sign that the courts must do better. Everyone in Nigeria deserves a fair day in court.

articles.title: 50 years of the Sex Pistols: not agents of chaos, but dreamers of a utopia
articles.author: John Schofield, Associate Professor, Archaeology, Flinders University; University of York
paras: On November 26 1976, a London-based punk band released a record that created shock waves around the world.

While not the first punk single to be released (The Damned’s New Rose, Radio Birdman’s Burn my Eye EP, and I’m Stranded by the Saints were released a few weeks earlier), Anarchy in the UK, by the Sex Pistols set the tone and a high bar for what was to follow.
With its snarling lyrics (“I am an antichrist”) and raw sound, the song blew a gaping hole in 1970s complacency.
The Sex Pistols are often thought to be obnoxious anarchists who promoted chaos. But in many ways they were the opposite.
Here are five ways they created a template for a more inclusive, more tolerant, and better balanced society that remains relevant in today’s uncertain world.
1. Social and political convention
Like many parts of the developed world, Britain in the mid-1970s faced economic decline, industrial unrest and growing disillusionment with established institutions.

Anarchy in the UK, followed by the band’s next single, God Save the Queen, released during Queen Elizabeth II’s Silver Jubilee in 1977, voiced the anger and alienation of many people while raising questions about national authority and identity.
The Pistols opened a door for many young people, inviting them to challenge established regimes, and to say no.
Their assertion that there was “no future” is also relevant today.
Alongside their strong influence on music, the Pistols heavily influenced style and fashion.

It is sometimes claimed the Pistols were conceived as a vehicle for Vivienne Westwood’s iconic clothing, which included bondage wear. As well as wearing her clothes, the band also took their name from her shop SEX on Chelsea’s Kings Road in London.
Westwood’s punk stylings encouraged others to create distinctive clothes and outfits from everyday and discarded items, including bin-bags and safety pins.
Based on her work with the Sex Pistols, and their manager Malcolm McLaren, Westwood’s career as a fashion iconoclast continued until her death in 2022.

Elsewhere, graphic designer Jamie Reid’s combination of “ransom note” typography and situationist style détournement has had a lasting effect on graphic art and design, while the filmic work of Julien Temple (who made the Sex Pistols 1980 film The Great Rock ‘n’ Roll Swindle) has heavily influenced the development of the rock biopic.
One of the Pistols main influences was in the emergence of a DIY approach to music.

This is perhaps epitomised in the Pistols infamous gig at the Lesser Free Trade Hall in Manchester on June 4 1976, which inspired attendees to form their own bands (famously: Joy Division, Buzzcocks and The Smiths).
In this, the myth that the Pistols “couldn’t play” simply inspired the realisation that anyone could pick up a guitar and make a record.
This DIY approach also involved the dissemination and promotion of music and the artists, through home-made fanzines, the precursor to the blogs and zines that proliferate today.
The Pistols encouraged women to become musicians.
Siouxsie Sioux was a member of the Pistols entourage, the Bromley Contingent, contributing to the chaos of the Sex Pistols’ infamous TV confrontation with Bill Grundy before founding the Banshees.

Palmolive and Viv Albertine of the Slits were previously members of the (unrecorded) Flowers of Romance along with John Ritchie (aka Sid Vicious). Chrissie Hynde, who had worked at SEX, went on to form The Pretenders. Poly Styrene was inspired to form X-Ray Spex having seen an early Pistols gig in Hastings in 1975.
The Pistols were central to a London punk scene that embraced and promoted diversity and difference at a time of racial tensions and intolerance.
The Pistols soon found fans across the world, including in many countries in the Soviet orbit, where their anti-establishment pronouncements found a resonance among disaffected youth.

In Indonesia, the circulation of semi-legal cassette tapes, and the few music publications tolerated by President Suharto’s “New Order” ultimately inspired an anarcho punk scene typified by Bandung band Runtah.
Thriving punk scenes have developed across the globe from Brazil to Japan, from Australia to the Arctic.

At a downtown bar in Perth, Australia, decades after the Sex Pistols first performed, another punk band rattle through their electrifying and energetic set to an adoring and enthusiastic audience. Pogoing may have evolved into moshing, but otherwise much remains the same.
Amyl and the Sniffers are among the latest in a long line of bands from around the world to have embraced the spirit of punk and the Pistols, carrying the legacy to a new generation of audiences.
This article draws on The Routledge Handbook of the Sex Pistols, edited by the authors with Mike Dines and Gabriela Gelain.

articles.title: Recent sinking of Russian vessels abroad shows the Russia-Ukraine war has officially gone global
articles.author: James Horncastle, Associate Professor and Edward and Emily McWhinney Professor in International Relations, Simon Fraser University
paras: Ukraine has been executing a series of successful strikes against Russian assets around the world. Ukrainian forces disabled a Russian cargo vessel off the coast of Finland, and sunk a Russian corvette, the Merkury, along with damaging another cargo vessel, in Libyan waters.
These attacks, in the aftermath of Ukraine’s severe damage to the Kerch Strait Bridge in Russian-occupied Crimea, have created hope among Ukraine’s allies.

The year 2026 hasn’t advanced Ukraine’s goal of ending the war. A stagnant battlefront, increased Russian aerial attacks and a recalcitrant American president have increased the burdens on Ukraine’s government and its people.
Russia hasn’t had a good year either. More than 400,000 Russians have been killed in the war — and potentially as many as 700,000.
For Ukraine to have any chance of winning, it must increase the pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s government. Making Russian assets vulnerable globally is one way to do it.
The international dimension

Since its outset, the Russia-Ukraine conflict has had an international dimension. Ukraine’s allies, both prior to and after Russia’s full-fledged invasion in 2022, rushed supplies to Ukraine in its moment of need.
Providing aid to Ukraine has continued for the past four years, despite disruptions caused by United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in the negotiation process.

The supplies provided by Ukraine’s allies are critical to its success. While the fighting is conducted by the Ukrainian people and Ukraine has increased domestic arms production, outside supplies are crucial in a number of areas — notably, air defence.

Equally important is the economic aid Ukraine’s allies have and continue to provide the country. Given the size differential between Russia and Ukraine and how hard the war has hit the Ukrainian economy, economic aid allows Ukraine to provide basic services to its citizens.

Initially, Russia did not court outside support to the same extent as Ukraine, as it believed it would achieve a rapid victory over its adversary. Once the reality of the conflict became clear, Russia turned to the international community for support.
That support has taken many forms. Iran and North Korea have been among Russia’s top supporters, providing drones and soldiers.

Other countries, most notably China, have provided an economic lifeline to Russia, allowing it access to their markets in an effort to stave off the worst impacts of the economic sanctions Ukraine’s allies have imposed on the Russians.
Countries in Central Asia and the Middle East have also served Russia as important intermediaries for acquiring sanctioned materials.

In a conflict that is increasingly defined by attrition, it’s been necessary for both Ukraine and Russia to rally their allies. The demands of industrialized warfare and the production of necessary armaments means neither country can produce what’s needed on their own.

Because both sides are receiving critical support in this industrialized conflict, the war has reached an equilibrium. In their current states, neither side is likely to achieve a decisive breakthrough to rapidly end the fighting.
For both Ukraine and Russia, that means targeting their adversary’s international allies is necessary to win the conflict.
The least risky form of targeting enemy support, and among the most important, is by constructing narratives while delegitimizing those of your opponent.

Ukraine has focused on Russia’s aggression and its violation of international norms and laws. The focus on international law is particularly important for Ukraine given Russian accusations that the West has flouted international norms for decades; Russia uses western association with Ukraine to gain support in the Global South.

Russia has put forward several narratives to justify the war, ranging from defending itself from NATO imperialist expansion to its factually questionable claims of the Ukrainian state’s genocide against ethnic Russians in Ukraine.
Russia had some early successes from these narratives, making political gains in Africa and earning support among far-right European parties.

Narrative campaigns, however, typically unfold over a long time frame. As both Ukraine and Russia seek immediate ways to boost morale and undermine their adversary, direct military operations abroad have become all the more significant.
Attacking the secure ‘rear’
In military terms, the rear is the area furthest from the enemy and ideally secure from military threat. For both Ukraine and Russia, this area has been other countries.
While Russia and Ukraine cannot attack the assets of other countries directly, they can and do engage in espionage against other countries.

For Russia, these efforts have focused on destabilizing Europe using drones and other assets via attacks that that are easily deniable. Russia also seeks to create pressure through violating European air space. The more Russia destabilizes Europe, Ukraine’s primary ally, the better its chances in the conflict.

For Ukraine, Russia’s aspirations to be a so-called Great Power mean its network is global — so Ukrainian special operation forces and intelligence agencies strike at Russian assets abroad where possible. These range from attacks in nearby areas, like the Baltics, to Africa and beyond.

While news agencies view this development as widening the conflict, and the United Nations may wish to prevent the conflict from going global, the reality is it’s been a global conflict since before 2022.
The strikes in Libya and the Baltic, and Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediate acknowledgement of Ukraine’s role, is just making it public.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s controversial return to Nvidia poses the question – what’s the point of a board?
articles.author: Anish Purkayastha, Senior lecturer, University of Sydney
paras: It’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom.
Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage.
Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him.
This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump.
Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power.
If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for?

Sometimes, the “hero” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage.
This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one.
Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession.

Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term.
Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement.

So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them.
It’s designed to solve something economists call the “principal-agent problem”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals).

That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams.
Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency.
Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished.

The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”.

We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced.

On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent.
But these rules fall short in three ways.
First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”.
In 2024, a US court found several Tesla directors who approved Elon Musk’s pay deal were too close to him to be independent. A higher court later restored the deal on other grounds.
Second, directors get much of their information from the very executive team they are meant to be keeping in check.
And third, a board without its own independent leader often struggles to push back against a chief executive. Nvidia only appointed its first-ever board chair on the day Huang resigned.
Why no one should be irreplaceable
“Key person” risk can’t be removed, but it can be managed.
Boards can train a credible successor, appoint an independent chair before a crisis hits, and finish investigations before deciding. They should also explain their reasoning in public.
An independent board that isn’t able to fire and replace a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be.

This matters well beyond Silicon Valley. Many retirement funds around the world own shares in Nvidia. For the sake of protecting millions of people’s long-term savings, retirement funds and others representing shareholders should be advocating for better governance than we’ve seen at Nvidia so far.

articles.title: In Kyrgyzstan, public meetings with the president turn into a quest to seek justice
articles.author: Nurbek Bekmurzaev
paras: Complaints include marriage disputes, unfair trial, unlawful land grabs, corruption, torture, and more
Originally published on Global Voices
An old man in the Talas province addressing Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov during a public meeting. Photo from the Presidential Administration's website. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In October and November 2026, Kyrgyzstan’s president, Sadyr Japarov, held public meetings with the population in all seven provinces of the country. What were meant to be formal events turned into quests for justice by people driven to desperation.
The meetings revealed the ineffectiveness of the existing justice mechanisms and showed how people saw the president as the only guarantor of justice.

The effectiveness of Kyrgyzstan’s law enforcement and judicial bodies was people’s most common justice-related complaint. During a meeting with residents of the southwestern Batken province on October 11, a woman complained to the president about her former husband, who accused her of forging their marriage certificate and framed her for crimes she did not commit to avoid the division of assets after their divorce.

She also said her former brother-in-law provided false testimony to back up his brother’s accusations. She now lives in an apartment with their three children in constant fear that her former husband may kick them out because he allegedly bribed police and courts.

This trivial legal dispute reached the point where the woman had to beg the president to ensure a just investigation and ruling. Japarov condemned her former husband and said that he should have left everything to her and their kids after the divorce.
Here is an Instagram reel with his response to the case.
View this post on Instagram

On October 26, Japarov met with residents of the Kazarman district in the southern Jalalabad province, where Shirimbek Abrahmanov told the president about his father, who was imprisoned for allegedly offering a bribe of KGS 2,000 (USD 23) to a police officer during a traffic stop. The district court acquitted him of the charges.
However, the local prosecutor’s office appealed the decision in the provincial court, which found Abdrahmanov’s father guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison.
Here is an Instagram reel with the complaint and Japarov’s response.
View this post on Instagram
Japarov could not hide his anger when he heard the story, especially after finding out the provincial court took seven months to issue a verdict. In reply, he confronted local authorities and said:

Are the traffic police officer and the prosecutor in cahoots? Does that mean they’ve ganged up on him? If it were a large bribe, that would be one thing. But to have someone imprisoned over two thousand soms — that’s a disgrace.
The man was released from custody shortly after Japarov’s intervention and subsequent pardon.
Similar complaints resurfaced multiple times during presidential meetings in other provinces, highlighting systemic problems plaguing the judicial and law-enforcement systems.
The message is clear: people have lost all hope of finding justice at the hands of local police and courts.

Surprisingly, following his meetings with the public, Japarov concluded that the level of distrust towards courts has decreased, but admitted that problems in the judicial system remain and must be solved quickly.

On the one hand, the lack of justice and the dysfunction within the courts and police bodies, which are plagued by corruption and bureaucracy, are real pressing issues affecting millions of people across Kyrgyzstan. However, the current political regime led by Japarov, who came to power in October 2020, has made little tangible progress.
In 2026, Kyrgyzstan was ranked 99th out of 144 states in the Rule of Law Index compiled by the World Justice Project. For comparison, in 2020, it was ranked 87th.

On the other hand, people’s desperate appeals for justice helped Japarov sustain his man-of-the-people image. By listening to people’s requests and swiftly resolving their issues, the president can reinforce his popularity. In turn, this leads to the maintenance of the personalistic regime built around Japarov since his arrival to power.

articles.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
articles.author: San Beauchemin, Doctoral Researcher, School of Political Studies, L’Université d’Ottawa/University of Ottawa
paras: By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life, the Rohingya faced restrictions on movement, education and health care while families were restricted to a two-child limit. Returning to Myanmar just to face the same conditions of life is not an option for many Rohingya.
The repatriation conundrum
It’s unlikely, however, that Myanmar will agree to grant citizenship to the Rohingya.
Since the 2021 coup d'état that ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi and her National League for Democracy, the military has had sole control of the government.

Earlier this year, Min Aung Hlaing, the architect of the Rohingya genocide who had been commander-in-chief of the Myanmar Forces since 2011, stepped down from his role and was subsequently elected president by a military-dominated parliament. This makes the prospect of a safe and dignified repatriation of the Rohingya to Myanmar a near impossibility.

The Myanmar military and government aren’t the only entities complicating the return of the Rohingya. Since late 2023, vast swaths of Rakhine state, where most Rohingya resided until 2017, have been under control of the Arakan army.

The army is the largest and most powerful non-state armed group in the country and it is vying for the independence of the Arakan region, where Rakhine is located. The Arakan army is openly hostile to the Rohingya, and those residing in the territory it controls are facing many of the same restrictions that were previously imposed by the state.
The ICJ established Myanmar’s responsibility for the genocide, and consequently ordered it to provide reparations and compensation, with details still to be decided.

But, in practice, there is little the court can do to compel Myanmar to take accountability and pursue justice if it refuses to do so. The ICJ has no independent enforcement mechanism; it only relies on states’ willingness to obey international law.
Only the United Nations Security Council could decide to take coercive action against Myanmar, but China and Russia, which both hold veto power, are likely to oppose it.

The two states have provided Min Aung Hlaing’s regime with political, diplomatic and military support over the years. Each also has its own issues with international human rights law, namely Russia’s war in Ukraine and China’s treatment of the Uyghurs.
How the ruling might help the Rohingya

The ICJ ruling has brought much-needed attention to the plight of the Rohingya. Renewed interest in the Rohingya crisis is expected to draw donations that could help alleviate some of the more pressing needs.

Funding for the refugee camps has dwindled in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic and the dismantlement of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID). Currently, the Rohingya in Bangladesh only receive US$7-$12 per person per month in food assistance.
Combined with the lack of income-generating opportunities, the cuts to food rations are frequently identified by refugees as the most severe challenge they face in the camps.

More attention could also result in stronger political pressure, not just on Myanmar but also on its regional partners. Malaysia, for example, began deporting refugees back to Myanmar in September 2026.

Since the government continues to deny access to international agencies for the refugees, including the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, it could not be verified whether these returns were voluntary, as Malaysia claimed.

It’s unlikely the Rohingya, who make up the majority of Myanmar refugees in Malaysia, are returning of their own free will. International pressure could force Malaysia to stop the deportations and avoid causing further harm to its already vulnerable Rohingya refugee community.

Finally, the most immediate benefit of the ruling is that, for the first time, there is a formal recognition of the Rohingya as a distinct people. The ruling directly contradicts Myanmar’s assertions that the Rohingya are “illegal immigrants from Bangladesh” who have no legitimate claim to rights and land in Rakhine.

The ICJ ruling clearly affirms that the atrocities the Rohingya have suffered are indeed genocide, and while it doesn’t guarantee justice for the Rohingya, it’s a necessary precondition that opens the path to restorative justice.
San Beauchemin is a member of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

articles.title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
articles.author: Mark Turin, Associate professor, Institute for Critical Indigenous Studies, University of British Columbia
paras: In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.
“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.
Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.
A country of 124 mother tongues
Nepal is one of the most linguistically diverse countries in the world, though the state has not always acknowledged it. The 2021 census recorded 124 mother tongues.

Fifty years earlier, in 1971, when the Panchayat regime was promoting Nepali above all other languages, the census counted just 17 languages. Today, Nepali is the first language of just under 45 per cent of the population.

I have worked in Nepal since 1991, first as a volunteer schoolteacher and later as a linguist and anthropologist. I have spent decades researching the country’s linguistic diversity. The census numbers reflect a shift I have witnessed on the ground, in communities.

In 2021, for the first time, the census asked people about their ancestral language as well as their mother tongue. Nearly three million more people name Nepali as their mother tongue than they name it as their ancestral language, a sign that many families have shifted to Nepali.
For other languages, the gap goes the other way. Some 300,000 more people name Nepal Bhasa, the language of the Newar community, as their ancestral language than name it as their mother tongue.

Nepali is also spreading as a second language: 46 per cent of the population now speaks it that way, up from 33 per cent in 2011. Whatever pressures Nepal’s other languages face, Nepali is certainly not a language at risk.
On paper, Nepal’s laws side with children. The government’s School Education Sector Plan 2022-32 commits to scaling up early-grade teaching in children’s mother tongues.

In practice, implementation has been sluggish and uneven. As comparative education scholar Uma Pradhan has shown, policy has long treated mother tongues as a bridge to Nepali, a stepping stone to be left behind, with the state offering little support.

In a 2026 study from Tanahun, one grandparent spoke about a granddaughter in Grade 2 who was being taught only in Nepali and English: “She [does not have the] opportunity to study in [her ancestral] language; so, there is a gap.”
The evidence for local languages

A 2024 study commissioned by UNICEF Nepal examined language use in 30 schools across all seven provinces. Its conclusion was unequivocal. When children learn in their mother tongue or a familiar language, they take a more active part in lessons and do better in assessments and exams.

Many schools have rushed to switch to English-language teaching, often for financial reasons and with little teacher training. Yet students taught in Nepali outscored their English-taught peers in Nepali, in science and even in English, according to the study’s analysis of school assessment results, which was limited in scale.

In Dailekh, in western Nepal, principal Sher Bahadur Rana told UNICEF that teachers once corrected children who used their own “language or dialect.” After training in multilingual teaching, he said, “we learned that children learn faster and feel more confident when we teach them in the language they speak and understand best.”
Obstacles to implementation

A recent review by education researchers Pariksha Onta and Amado Padilla, covering 111 studies and policy documents, points to a “persistent disconnect between constitutional commitments, classroom practice and targeted funding.”

Where mother tongues are taught at all, they are usually a subject rather than the language children learn in. Textbooks in children’s mother tongues remain scarce, and most of those that do exist are translations of Nepali materials with little locally relevant content. Far too few teachers who speak local languages are recruited or trained.

Parents, meanwhile, are caught in the middle. Many see English-language schools as a marker of quality and employability. And funding is lacking: in 2026–27, education and sports together received around 10.3 per cent of Nepal’s national budget, well below the international benchmark of allocating at least 15 per cent to education.

Onta and Padilla’s review also highlights what works. In some Kathmandu Valley schools, children learn in Nepal Bhasa for their first three grades before Nepali and English are phased in. A strong foundation in the mother tongue supports learning in the other languages, which means families don’t have to choose between them.
As I argued previously with colleagues Lava Deo Awasthi and Yogendra Prasad Yadava, rights “do not implement themselves.”

Children should begin school in the language they understand best, with Nepali and English introduced gradually, building on that foundation. Making this work requires sustained funding, teachers trained to teach in children’s languages, and materials that reflect their lives and communities.
Some municipalities have introduced local-language education programs, while Nepal’s Curriculum Development Centre has developed curricula for elementary education in more than 20 mother tongues.

Language policy can sound technical, but at heart it is about whether a child’s first experience of school is a welcoming one. In Renuka Dahal’s classroom in Rautahat, where children now teach their teacher, the message is simple: their languages belong in school, and so do they.
Mark Turin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (SSHRC).

articles.title: Climate summits need radical reform – here’s how to transform global negotiations
articles.author: Francesco Grillo, Academic Fellow, Department of Social and Political Sciences, Bocconi University
paras: The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.
Where could that start? What kind of alliance does such a reform need? A recent conference on the global governance of climate change provides some answers.

Cop has probably been killed by a contradiction. The first Cop in 1995 – chaired by Angela Merkel, then Germany’s young environment minister – was regulated by a UN law. This was the Framework Convention on Climate Change, which envisaged that decisions had to be taken by consensus or, if that wasn’t possible, by two-thirds of the parties (each state of the world is a “party”). This law, known as draft rule 42, was never accepted or rejected, leaving Cop trapped in the unanimity trap.

In 2010, this was enough for Bolivia alone to object to risk derailing the entire negotiation. It is a trap because countries have naturally different interests. Most developing countries are highly exposed to climate change and do not contribute much to the problem; some others not only benefit from oil production but also from global warming itself (notably Russia, as Arctic trade routes open up due to ice melting).

Most other traditional UN institutions do not operate under such strict consensus: the General Assembly (the main policymaking body of the UN), Unesco (the UN’s Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation) and the World Health Organization all vote with a qualified two-thirds majority on important matters.

So unanimity must be abolished. But that is not enough. Cop also manages to be both inefficient and not inclusive enough of the actors that matter a lot in achieving the goals of a climate change agenda. The parties include the tiny country of San Marino yet there’s no representation from megacities like Mumbai or Seattle – cities which may be exposed to climate disaster and host some of the solutions.

A new annual conference called Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels was a significant attempt to move beyond the Cop gridlock. In 2026, 57 countries joined the first meeting in Santa Marta, Colombia after realising at Cop30 last year in Brazil, that, by “consensus”, Cop cannot even agree on the need for a roadmap to end dependence on fossil fuels. And yet even shrinking the number of parties to a quarter of Cop’s total was not enough to get beyond the acknowledgement of such a necessity: the final document did not indicate any timeline nor commit countries to specific targets.
